newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl allies debate balanced budgets, low tax.
newsitem.headline: Kohl allies debate balanced budgets, low tax.

text.p: Germany's liberal Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, on Saturday debated whether to adopt a programme demanding constitutional changes to ensure balanced budgets and low taxes.

A party congress in this central spa town was due to vote on the "Wiesbaden Principles", the culmination of a move by the FDP over the past few years to focus on free market economic values such as privatisation and deregulation, later in the day.

The programme calls for changes in the German constitution to oblige all levels of public administration to achieve balanced budgets within ten years and to limit the average tax burden to one third of an individual's income.

FDP officials said the programme, proposed by the national leadership and already widely discussed in local party branches, was almost certain to be adopted with only the section on balanced budgets likely to provoke serious opposition.
"The new FDP is a reform party fighting for more freedom and responsibility for the individual," general secretary Guido Westerwelle told around 660 delegates at the congress.

Westerwelle said the FDP, which provides Kohl with his 12-seat parliamentary majority, would use the programme in a drive to become Germany's third party -- its traditional postwar status which it has lost to the environmentalist Greens.
"We want to reconquer third place in the party structure with distinctive policies. Simply helping another party to gain a majority is too little to be worth fighting for," he said.
Opinion polls show the FDP hovering around the five percent barrier a party must overcome to be represented in parliament.
Westerwelle said the way to cut Germany's unemployment total of more than four million was to roll back the frontiers of the state to and place a greater emphasis on private enterprise.
Pointless regulations were stifling the formation of new businesses and frustrating a new generation of young entrepreneurs in the mould of Microsoft founder Bill Gates, Westerwelle said.
"Bill Gates wouldn't have been possible in Germany," he said. "He began his business in a garage -- and a garage doesn't have a window and two separate toilets."

Westerwelle said the FDP, which has styled itself as the champion of lower taxes within Kohl's coalition, would continue this policy despite looming budget shortfalls for 1997 and the next few years. General elections are due in 1998.

"The subject of tax is a question of freedom for us," he said. "When more than every second deutschemark is passing through the hands of the state, that means there is too little of the market economy, not too much."
